title: What is token-based authentication — server issues a token (JWT), client sends it in Authorization header, server validates without storing state — and why is it better for microservices (stateless, scalable)?
shortTitle: Token-Based Authentication (JWT) and Why It Suits Microservices

s1_definition.profdef: Token-based authentication is a stateless scheme in which, after login, the server issues a signed, self-contained token (commonly a JWT) carrying the user's identity and claims. The client stores the token and sends it on each request, typically in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. The server validates the token purely by checking its cryptographic signature and expiry; it keeps no per-user session on the server. Because no shared server state is required, any instance can validate any token.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of writing Rajesh's details in a central register, National Bank of India gives him a tamper-proof stamped passbook page that already contains his name, his account type, and an expiry date, all sealed with the bank's official stamp. Any branch can look at the page, verify the stamp is genuine, read the details right there, and serve him — without phoning head office. No branch needs to remember Rajesh; the proof travels with him.
s1_definition.oneliner: The token carries the identity inside itself, signed by the server, so any server can trust it without looking anything up.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Token-based authentication is a stateless scheme in which, after login, the server issues a signed, self-contained token (commonly a JWT) carrying the user's identity and claims. The client stores the token and sends it on each request, typically in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. The server validates the token purely by checking its cryptographic signature and expiry; it keeps no per-user session on the server. Because no shared server state is required, any instance can validate any token.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Instead of writing Rajesh's details in a central register, National Bank of India gives him a tamper-proof stamped passbook page that already contains his name, his account type, and an expiry date, all sealed with the bank's official stamp. Any branch can look at the page, verify the stamp is genuine, read the details right there, and serve him — without phoning head office. No branch needs to remember Rajesh; the proof travels with him.

**One line to remember:** The token carries the identity inside itself, signed by the server, so any server can trust it without looking anything up.

sections.s2_technical:
On login the server builds and signs a JWT, for example with the io.jsonwebtoken library: `Jwts.builder().subject("rajesh").claim("role","CUSTOMER").expiration(exp).signWith(key).compact()`. The client stores it and sends it as `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...`. On each request the server validates it: `Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build().parseSignedClaims(token)` throws if the signature is wrong or the token is expired, otherwise it returns the claims, and the server trusts them without a database lookup.

Why this fits microservices: it is stateless and horizontally scalable. In a system with an Order Service, an Account Service, and a Settlement Service, each can independently verify the same token using a shared public key or secret — there is no central session store to become a bottleneck or single point of failure. Adding a new instance requires zero session replication. For example, the Account Service reads the role claim with `claims.get("role")` and enforces its own authorization locally.

The senior nuance is the trade-off: because validation is local and the token is self-contained, you cannot easily revoke a token before it expires. A stolen token is valid until expiry. Mitigations are short-lived access tokens (15 minutes) plus refresh tokens, and a server-side denylist of revoked token IDs (jti) checked for high-risk actions, which reintroduces a little state. Also, claims are only Base64-encoded, not encrypted, so sensitive data must never go in the payload.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has split its monolith into three microservices. When Rajesh logs in once, all three services must recognize him without each one calling a central session database on every request, because that database would melt under the load. This is exactly how token-based auth helps — Rajesh gets a signed token that every service can verify on its own.

Problem 2 — On a busy trading day the bank spins up five extra Account Service instances in seconds. These brand-new instances have never seen Rajesh, yet they must serve his requests immediately. This is exactly why stateless tokens scale — a fresh instance only needs the shared signing key, not a copy of anyone's session.

Our mini-project builds a `TokenService` that issues and validates signed tokens (HMAC here, kept simple), and a demo where an issued token is validated by two independent service instances, plus a tampered token is rejected and an expired token is rejected.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run
javac TokenDemo.java
java com.bank.token.TokenDemo

# Spring Boot microservice
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/token-auth-service-1.0.0.jar

# Call a protected endpoint across services with the same bearer token
TOKEN=$(curl -s -d 'user=rajesh&pass=secret123' http://localhost:8080/login)
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a login for user "rajesh" with role "CUSTOMER" and a 15-minute TTL.

Step 1: `issue("rajesh","CUSTOMER",900)` builds the payload "rajesh|CUSTOMER|exp", Base64-encodes it, computes an HMAC signature over it, and returns `payload.signature`. The token is self-contained — the identity now lives inside it.

Step 2: Account Service instance one calls `validate(token)`. It recomputes the HMAC and compares; it matches, and the expiry is in the future, so it returns claims username "rajesh", role "CUSTOMER". No database was touched.

Step 3: A brand-new Settlement Service instance calls `validate(token)` on the same token. Because it holds the same shared secret, it too verifies the signature and reads the claims. This proves any instance can validate without shared session state.

Step 4: A tampered token (last characters changed) fails the signature comparison, so `validate` throws. An expired token (negative TTL) passes the signature check but fails the expiry check, so it also throws. Both map to HTTP 401.

```text
2026-10-31 22:40:00.010 INFO    [TokenDemo] Issued token for rajesh (role=CUSTOMER)
2026-10-31 22:40:00.012 INFO    [TokenDemo] Account Service #1 validated -> user=rajesh, role=CUSTOMER
2026-10-31 22:40:00.013 INFO    [TokenDemo] Settlement Service (new instance) validated -> user=rajesh
2026-10-31 22:40:00.014 SEVERE  [TokenDemo] Tampered token rejected: bad signature
2026-10-31 22:40:00.015 SEVERE  [TokenDemo] Expired token rejected: token expired
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Client login: POST /login {rajesh}
    │
    ▼
  Auth Server
    │ sign(payload) → JWT
    │ return token (client stores it)
    ▼
  Client sends: Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
    │
    ├────────────────┬─────────────────┐
    ▼                ▼                 ▼
  Account Svc #1   Settlement Svc    (future new instance)
    │ verify sig    │ verify sig    │ only needs shared key
    │ check exp     │ check exp     │ no session store
    ▼                ▼                 ▼
  200 OK           200 OK            200 OK
  (no DB lookup for identity — fully stateless)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — TokenService ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Applied ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TokenService only issues/validates tokens            │
  │  O: swap HMAC → RSA by changing sign() only              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │        TokenService          │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ - secret: String             │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + issue(user,role,ttl):String│
  │ + validate(token): TokenClaims│  throws InvalidTokenException
  │ - sign(data): String         │  HMAC-SHA256
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                  │ produces
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ TokenClaims {username, role,  │
  │   expiresAt}                  │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  State: ISSUED ──exp passes──→ EXPIRED (validate → 401)
         ISSUED ──tampered──→ INVALID (validate → 401)

  Contract for validate(token):
    Post: returns claims if signature valid AND not expired
    Throws: InvalidTokenException on bad signature or expiry
    Trade-off: no instant revocation → use short TTL + jti denylist
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Token-based authentication is a stateless scheme where, after login, the server issues a signed, self-contained token such as a JWT that carries the user's identity and claims. The client stores it and sends it on every request in the Authorization Bearer header. The server validates the token by checking its signature and expiry alone, keeping no session on the server, which means any instance can verify any token.

In my banking project we moved from a session monolith to microservices, and token-based auth was the key enabler. When Rajesh logs in once he gets a signed token, and the Order Service, Account Service, and Settlement Service each verify it independently using a shared signing key. There is no central session database for every request to hammer, so we removed a major bottleneck and single point of failure.

The scalability benefit is concrete: on a busy trading day we spin up extra Account Service instances in seconds, and because they only need the signing key, they can serve Rajesh immediately without any session replication. In my demo I showed one issued token being validated by two separate service instances, and I showed that a tampered token fails the signature check and an expired token fails the expiry check, both returning 401.

The trade-off I always raise is revocation. Because validation is local and the token is self-contained, a stolen token stays valid until it expires. We handle this with short-lived access tokens of about fifteen minutes backed by refresh tokens, and for high-risk actions we check a small server-side denylist of revoked token ids. I also stress that JWT claims are only Base64-encoded, not encrypted, so we never put sensitive data like balances in the payload.
